newsitem.title: USA: For some US energy cos domestic buys too expensive.
newsitem.headline: For some US energy cos domestic buys too expensive.

text.p: The prospect of deregulation of the U.S. energy supply industry has inspired a wave of mergers among gas companies and electricity utilities, but some believe the cost of domestic acquisitions is too high.

"Deals are coming in every day but if that deal does not produce 15 percent retrun on equity we are not interested and in domestic power generation we so not see that," MCN Corp vice chairman William McCrackin told a conference on Tuesday.

Deals such as last week's $2.0 billion merger of Kansas City Power and Light Co and Western Resources have come to the fore as electricity producers and distributors scurry for allies ahead of the end of their protected market.
Instead, energy companies such as Michigan-based MCN and CMS Energy Corp, which produce, transport and distribute natural gas and electricity are looking overseas to generate future earnings streams.

MCN, which had operating revenues of $608 billion in 1996, says that it has built succesful investments in India by using a local partner, an experience which compares favourably with giant Enron Corp's Dhabol power plant in the western Indian state of Maharashtra which ran foul of economic nationalism.

"We are a low key player in India, no-one is going to read about us in the press, but we plan to invest $400-500 million in 10-12 Indian power projects which will generate 25 percent returns," said McCrackin.
Michael Morris of CMS said he was being offered more overseas deals than he could say grace over.
He noted that going overseas was the only way CMS could grow earnings 10 percent a year and an produe an overall return of 15 percent for investors.
"The domestic marketplace is simply too competitive to generate the kinds of returns for the capital investment required in the electric utility industry," said Morris.
The company's electricity division, which has 1.5 million customers in Michigan, is projected to generate 2.2 percent growth annually for the next 10 years.
In order to bolster shareholder returns, CMS aims to get 35-40 percent of the CMS operating earnings from overseas by the year 2001, compared with just 19 percent now.
"We are seeing tremendous success and rates of return internationally that we simply do not see in our electric utilities back home," Morris said.
CMS which has an energy joint venture in Argentina also aims to build a 560 mile high-pressure gas pipeline to supply the copper producing region of northern Chile.

"We are going beyond Argentina, where we are the second largest U.S. investor, and the president of our company has just completed a series of succesful meetings with the president of Chile, Eduardo Frei," Morris said.

CMS also has a strong presence in Morocco and Morris said that the company will soon be the country's largest producer of electricity and the company was looking at Ghana, Equatorial Guinea and Tunisia in the region.
In Asia, it recently bought in to a Philippine electricity utility.
"But when you look at buys in the domestic U.S., you will see us on the sidelines," he said. ((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
